title: Section check: Objects, making and power
intro: 10 questions about Lessons 1–5. Take your time. You can look back at the lessons and try again as often as you like.

questions.question: Hokusai's wave print has many impressions. What is an impression?

options.text: A painting made for one room
options.feedback: Not quite. A painting for one room is like The Harvesters. An impression is one printed copy. Look back at Lesson 1.

options.text: One printed copy from the blocks
options.feedback: Yes. Many copies can be printed from the same wood blocks. Each copy is an impression.

options.text: The block of wood with the design
options.feedback: Not quite. The block holds the design. An impression is a copy printed on paper from it. Look back at Lesson 1.

questions.question: The Harvesters shows farm workers in 1565. Why can it not show the life of every farm worker?

options.text: It shows its rich patron's view.
options.feedback: Yes. A rich merchant in Antwerp ordered it for his house. The museum says the scene is nicer than real life.

options.text: It was painted by the farm workers.
options.feedback: Not quite. Bruegel painted it for a rich merchant in the city. The workers did not choose how they were shown. Look back at Lesson 1.

options.text: It is a print made for many buyers.
options.feedback: Not quite. The Harvesters is an oil painting on wood. It was made for one patron and one room. Look back at Lesson 1.

questions.question: In batik, melted wax is a resist. What does a resist do?

options.text: It makes all the colours much brighter.
options.feedback: Not quite. The dye gives the colour. The wax keeps the dye off some parts. Look back at Lesson 2.

options.text: It adds gold leaf to the whole cloth.
options.feedback: Not quite. Gold leaf is called prada. A resist keeps the dye off parts of the cloth. Look back at Lesson 2.

options.text: It keeps dye off part of the cloth.
options.feedback: Yes. The wax protects the parts the maker chooses. Then the dye colours the rest.

stimulus.title: A made-up museum label
stimulus.body: This is a made-up example. A museum shows a batik skirt from a town on the north coast of Java. It was made in the 1800s. Its label says: "This skirt shows what all Javanese people wore at that time."

questions.question: Which change would make this label more accurate?

options.text: Say it shows what all of Indonesia wore
options.feedback: Not quite. That makes the claim even bigger. One cloth cannot show what everyone wore. Look back at Lesson 2.

options.text: Say it shows one place's tradition
options.feedback: Yes. A cloth shows one place and its makers. It does not show what every Javanese person wore.

options.text: Take away the place where it was made
options.feedback: Not quite. The place helps explain the cloth. Places in Java had different traditions. Look back at Lesson 2.

questions.question: Why are ceramics useful evidence of links between places?

options.text: Fired clay lasts, and many were made.
options.feedback: Yes. Fired clay survives well. People made very many pots, so lots of them are left to study.

options.text: They were made only for rulers at court.
options.feedback: Not quite. Makers made everyday pots for many buyers, at home and far away. Look back at Lesson 3.

options.text: Each one tells us who bought it and where.
options.feedback: Not quite. The dish from the shipwreck does not tell us who bought it. Look back at Lesson 3.

questions.question: A bronze box made in China has Arabic writing on its lid. What can the box show us?

options.text: Who used the box in their home each day
options.feedback: Not quite. The box does not tell us who used it. Look back at Lesson 3.

options.text: That the box was sent to another country
options.feedback: Not quite. The writing does not prove the box went abroad. Look back at Lesson 3.

options.text: One object can link two traditions
options.feedback: Yes. It joins Chinese making with Arabic religious words. One place name cannot tell its whole story.

questions.question: The false beard on the sphinx was a convention. What is a convention?

options.text: A gift that people gave to a god
options.feedback: Not quite. Offerings were gifts. A convention is a usual way of showing something, like a king's false beard. Look back at Lesson 4.

options.text: A new idea that no one used before
options.feedback: Not quite. A convention is the opposite. It is a usual way that many people used. Look back at Lesson 4.

options.text: A usual way of showing something
options.feedback: Yes. Egyptian kings were usually shown with a false beard. Hatshepsut's images followed this way.

questions.question: How did the Moche ear ornament show that a person had high status?

options.text: Costly materials, skill, and wearing it
options.feedback: Yes. Gold, stones and shell, joined with skill, showed a person's rank on their body.

options.text: Its huge size, inside a temple building
options.feedback: Not quite. That is the sphinx. The ornament was small, and people wore it on the body. Look back at Lesson 4.

options.text: Writing on it that gives the owner's name
options.feedback: Not quite. The ornament shows a runner with wings. Its gold, stones and shell showed rank. Look back at Lesson 4.

stimulus.title: A made-up ruler's album
stimulus.body: This is a made-up example. Queen Tamsa collects fine pages. One page has writing made 100 years before her time. Her painters add new flower borders around it. Then the page goes into her album, next to new paintings.

questions.question: Which idea from Lesson 5 does this example show?

options.text: Only new pictures can go in an album.
options.feedback: Not quite. The Shah Jahan Album held old writing as well as new paintings. Look back at Lesson 5.

options.text: An album can give an old work a new setting.
options.feedback: Yes. Like Mir 'Ali Haravi's writing, the old page gets new borders in a new book.

options.text: Old writing must stay just as it was made.
options.feedback: Not quite. Mughal artists painted new borders around older writing. Look back at Lesson 5.

questions.question: In Akbar's House of Books, how was one painting often made?

options.text: Several specialists worked on it.
options.feedback: Yes. One artist might plan it, others add colour, and experts paint faces or animals.

options.text: One artist did every part alone.
options.feedback: Not quite. Painters worked with writers, decorators and bookbinders. Several people could work on one picture. Look back at Lesson 5.

options.text: The emperor painted it himself.
options.feedback: Not quite. Akbar was a patron. He ordered the work, and skilled makers made it. Look back at Lesson 5.

results.high: Well done. You know a lot about how objects connect to the people who made and used them.
results.middle: Good work. You remember many of the main ideas. Look back at any lesson you want to check.
results.low: Thank you for trying. Look back at Lessons 1–5, then try again whenever you like.
